title: SQL Transactions & ACID
oneLiner: A bank transfer is two UPDATEs. A transaction is what stops a crash between them from losing money.
keyTakeaway: Wrap statements that must succeed or fail together in BEGIN ... COMMIT. If anything goes wrong before COMMIT -- an error, a constraint violation, a crash -- ROLLBACK undoes all of it, so the database never shows the half-finished state. That all-or-nothing guarantee is the A in ACID.
explanation:
Moving $100 from Ava to Ben takes two statements: subtract from Ava, add to Ben. Run them one at a time and there is a moment where the money has left Ava's account but not reached Ben's. If the server crashes, the app throws, or the network drops in that moment, the $100 is simply gone. Bugs like this are rare per request and certain over enough requests.

A transaction groups statements into one unit. `BEGIN` starts it; nothing you change is final until `COMMIT`. If something fails first, `ROLLBACK` puts every row back exactly as it was at BEGIN -- and if the server dies mid-transaction, the database rolls it back on restart by itself. Other sessions never see the in-between state.

That's what ACID describes. Atomicity: all of it happens or none of it does. Consistency: rules like `CHECK (balance >= 0)` hold before and after, so a transfer that would overdraw an account is rejected outright. Isolation: two transactions running at once don't see each other's half-done work (how strictly is the isolation level -- READ COMMITTED is a common default, SERIALIZABLE the strictest). Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash.

In application code this is usually `using var tx = connection.BeginTransaction()` in C# (or your ORM's equivalent, an ORM being an object-relational mapper, a library that maps tables to classes; e.g. EF Core's `SaveChanges`, which wraps its batch in one), with a commit at the end and a rollback in the error path. Keep transactions short: while one is open it can hold locks other requests are waiting on.
